Finally, E. coli were log transformed to normalize the distribution, as it was heavily skewed. 10 This ensured that during model fitting that the model was not overly sensitive to large values with correspondingly large errors. 5.3.5 Train Model 5.3.5.1 Modeling approach Linear regression, adaptive lasso with diurnal model features, and XGBoost were used to predict iCT, E. coli concentrations, and E. coli removal. Linear regression represented a simplified baseline condition. Adaptive lasso is a linear regression method with built-in feature selection, and in this case sine and cosine terms were added as features to represent common diurnal trends in water and wastewater treatment. This was primarily to test potential time- dependent behavior that was observed in some water quality sensors. The ML approach that was explored was XGBoost, a tree-based approach in which each subsequent regression decision tree fit to the total error (residuals) of the previous trees. As a tree-based approach, XGBoost has been shown to be effective with (1) laboratory data that may include some measurement variability or noisy sensor data and (2) significantly different model output (response) behavior depending on the range of values. Model training included both random and time-based 5-fold cross validation of 80% of the data for model training and hyper-parameter tuning, with the remaining 20% for testing (Figure 5- 35). The most common practice of splitting training and testing data involves random sampling. However, because of the high autocorrelation of the E coli measurements, a time-series approach was deemed necessary. When a random train/test split was used with XGBoost, training and testing accuracy exceeded 91%. This was significantly reduced when the time- series approach was implemented suggesting that data leakage may have occurred during the random selection. The poor performance of models using the time-based split was also likely influenced by the small sample size (and lack of process variability) of the initial training windows. To remedy this, a second train-test split approach was explored. 68 The Water Research Foundation Figure 5-35. A cumulative distribution function (CDF)-based method was explored as an alternative train- test split approach. The goal of using a CDF split was to maximize the sample size used during training, minimize autocorrelation between samples, and maximize the range of values for an individual variable. A random sample from a uniform distribution was used to select training observations from an empirical CDF of all response variable observations; this ensured a wide range of values in the training set. The same 80%/20% train-test split was maintained. 5.3.5.2 Modeling results The inclusion of the E. coli analyzer provided sufficient information to overcome any sample size limitation and perform comparably to the same modeling approach with a larger sample size (Figure 5-36).
